name: Pattern formation

origin.note: Suzuki and Yamashita characterised the patterns that anonymous robots can form in terms of their initial configuration.

summary: Robots start at distinct points and must form a given geometric pattern, up to similarity; which patterns are formable, and from which initial configurations?
statement: $n$ robots start at distinct points of the plane. Each is given the same **pattern** $P$, a set (or multiset) of $n$ points in its own local coordinate system. The robots must reach a configuration similar to $P$ (equal up to translation, rotation, uniform scaling and, without **chirality** (a common clockwise direction), reflection) and stay there. The question is for which pairs (initial configuration, pattern) this is possible under the given assumptions, and at what cost in time and colours.

primer.intro: Picture drones at a light show that must arrange themselves into a picture, say a star, with no director and no radio. There are $n$ **robots**, tiny points at different places in the plane; the positions of all robots at one instant form a **configuration**. Each robot repeats a **Look–Compute–Move cycle**: it takes a **snapshot** of where the other robots are (Look), decides on a destination point (Compute) and moves towards it (Move). The robots are identical, silent and **oblivious** (they forget everything at the end of each cycle), and each one sees the world in its own **local coordinate system**, with its own origin, unit of length and directions. An adversary called the **scheduler** decides the **activation** of each robot, that is, when it performs a cycle; in the standard version (ASYNC) every phase may take any finite time, so a robot may look while others are still moving. All robots receive the same **pattern** $P$, a list of $n$ points, and must end in a configuration equal to $P$ up to shifting, turning, resizing and mirroring, and then stop; the question is from which initial configurations this is possible.

ideas.title: Elect a leader, then build a shared coordinate system from the smallest enclosing circle
ideas.idea:
1. Every robot computes the **smallest enclosing circle** (SEC): the smallest circle that contains all robots. It is the same circle for everyone, whatever their local coordinate systems.
2. The centre of the SEC becomes the common origin and its radius the common unit of length.
3. The robots elect a **leader**, a robot whose position in the configuration looks different from every other robot's (for example the only robot closest to the centre). The ray from the centre through the leader becomes the common \"east\"; because all robots agree on what clockwise means (**chirality**), this also fixes a common \"north\".
4. Now all robots use the shared coordinate system, so they all place the pattern $P$ in the same spot (scaled to the circle) and compute the same assignment of robots to points of $P$; the point assigned to a robot is its **target point**.
5. The robots move to their target points in a careful order that never changes the SEC and never lets another robot take over the leader's special position, so the shared coordinate system survives every move.
ideas.analysis: Once everyone agrees on coordinates, the task is just \"walk to your target point\"; the difficulty is step 5, because an oblivious robot recomputes everything in every cycle, and one careless move (a robot on the circle stepping inwards, say) can change the circle or the leader and with them every robot's target point. Dieudonné, Petit and Villain used this plan to show that, with chirality, pattern formation is solvable exactly when leader election is, for $n \ge 4$ robots in ASYNC [Dieudonne2010Leader]. The catalogue's current best drops chirality: arbitrary pattern formation is solvable exactly when a leader can be elected [Cicerone2019Asynchronous]. Running time is not analysed in these papers.
ideas.why_it_matters: It turned a geometric problem into a symmetry-breaking problem: forming any pattern is as hard as choosing one leader.

ideas.title: A symmetric initial configuration that the scheduler keeps symmetric forever
ideas.idea: Place $n = 4$ robots on the corners of a square and ask for a pattern that does not look the same after a quarter turn, for example four points on a line. The adversary gives each robot a local coordinate system with its origin at the robot, the $x$-axis pointing to the centre of the square, and the same unit; the four systems are then copies of each other turned by $90^\circ$. Every robot now gets exactly the same snapshot. The scheduler activates all four together. Identical robots with identical snapshots choose the same move in their own local coordinate systems, which in the real plane is the same move turned by $90^\circ$. So after these cycles the robots again form a square (or all stand at its centre), and the scheduler repeats this forever. The line is never formed.
ideas.analysis: The same argument works for any initial configuration that looks the same after some rotation: whatever the algorithm, the robots can only form patterns that keep at least that much symmetry. Suzuki and Yamashita measured this with the **symmetricity** of a configuration [Suzuki1999Formation]. The scheduler only needs to activate every robot at once, so the obstacle holds in the fully synchronous model (FSYNC) and therefore under every less synchronous scheduler. Hence, without any agreement between local coordinate systems, an arbitrary pattern cannot be formed from every initial configuration [Flocchini2008Arbitrary]; from a regular $n$-gon only a point and the regular $n$-gon itself can be formed [Flocchini2017Uniform].
ideas.why_it_matters: It explains why every pattern-formation result is about breaking symmetry, and why leader election keeps appearing.

ideas.title: With a common compass nobody is symmetric
ideas.idea:
Suppose all robots agree on north and east (a **common compass**), though not on origin or unit.

1. Each robot sorts all robots from west to east, and robots on the same north-south line from south to north. Since all robots agree on north and east, they all obtain the same order, even though their origins and units differ.
2. Each robot sorts the points of the pattern $P$ in the same way and matches the $i$-th robot with the $i$-th point of $P$, its target point, (after placing and scaling $P$ by a rule everyone computes alike).
3. The robots move in an order chosen so that the order of step 1, and hence the assignment of target points, does not change while they move.
ideas.analysis: A common compass removes the adversary's trick: no rotation or mirror image can map a set of points to itself while keeping north and east fixed, so every configuration has a first robot that all robots recognise. Flocchini, Prencipe, Santoro and Widmayer showed that with a common compass any number of robots form any pattern in ASYNC, and that agreement on one axis suffices for an odd number of robots [Flocchini2008Arbitrary]. The steps above are a simplified sketch that was not checked against that paper's full text; the fact that a compass gives all robots the same order is Lemma 2.1 of [Efrima2009Partition].
ideas.why_it_matters: It shows that symmetry, not obliviousness or asynchrony, is the real obstacle to forming patterns.

glossary.definition: a computing entity modelled as a point of the plane (a unit disc for fat robots); all robots run the same algorithm
the positions of all $n$ robots at one instant, a multiset of points of the plane

one activation of a robot: in Look it takes a snapshot, in Compute it determines a destination point from that snapshot alone (and its own light, where lights exist), in Move it travels towards that point
the configuration as a robot observes it in Look (with the colours of the lights it sees, where lights exist), expressed in its local coordinate system
a robot keeps no memory from one Look–Compute–Move cycle to the next: Compute uses only the current snapshot

the origin, axes, unit of length and handedness in which a robot expresses its snapshot and its destination; robots agree on none of these unless the setting assumes chirality, one common axis or a common compass

the adversary that decides when each robot is activated: FSYNC activates every robot in every round, SSYNC a nonempty subset of the robots in each round, the sequential scheduler exactly one robot per round, and ASYNC lets each phase of each cycle take any finite time; every robot is activated infinitely often
the scheduler's choice to let a robot perform one Look–Compute–Move cycle; a robot that is not activated stays still

the set (or multiset) $P$ of $n$ points that every robot receives in its local coordinate system; it is formed when the configuration is similar to $P$, that is, equal up to translation, rotation, uniform scaling and, without chirality, reflection
the unique smallest circle that contains a given finite set of points (by default the robots of the configuration), abbreviated SEC; it does not depend on any local coordinate system

a robot that every robot identifies as the same unique robot from its snapshot, whatever its local coordinate system (for example the only robot closest to the centre of the smallest enclosing circle)
the point of the pattern $P$, placed in the plane by a rule all robots compute alike, that the algorithm assigns to a robot as its final position
agreement of all robots on the clockwise direction (handedness) of their local coordinate systems, with no agreement on axes, unit or origin
agreement of all robots on the direction and orientation of both axes of their local coordinate systems (north and east), not on unit or origin

history: The founding question was **which patterns robots can form at all** [Suzuki1999Formation]: Suzuki and Yamashita characterised formable patterns by the symmetry of the starting configuration, for SSYNC robots with unbounded memory and common handedness: only a point and a regular $n$-gon can be formed from every starting configuration. Flocchini, Prencipe, Santoro and Widmayer then asked the question that shaped the field, **how much agreement is needed**: none is not enough, one axis is enough for an odd number of robots, two axes for all [Flocchini1999Hard] [Flocchini2008Arbitrary]. The aim has been to remove assumptions one at a time (chirality, synchrony, rigidity), ending in the equivalence with leader election without chirality [Cicerone2019Asynchronous].

measures.name: Time
measures.description: rounds (FSYNC, SSYNC) or epochs (ASYNC) until the task is done; "finite" when only solvability is known

measures.name: Colours
measures.description: colours of the light per robot (0 for oblivious robots)

variants.title: ASYNC, no agreement on coordinates
variants.summary: Without any common orientation, an arbitrary pattern can be formed exactly from the configurations in which a leader can be elected.

preconditions: for some initial configurations: symmetric configurations cannot be broken by oblivious deterministic robots

results.note: Introduces arbitrary pattern formation for asynchronous oblivious robots and shows that with no common agreement an arbitrary pattern cannot be formed in general.

Characterisation: arbitrary pattern formation is solvable exactly when leader election is, in ASYNC without chirality. The paper also states that earlier proofs ([Fujinaga2015Pattern], [Bramas2016Probabilistic], the arXiv version of [Dieudonne2010Leader]) are not correct.

time.note: Time is not analysed in these papers.

open: Bound the number of epochs needed by an arbitrary pattern formation algorithm in ASYNC; no time analysis is recorded.
variants.notes: Patterns are formed up to translation, rotation, scaling and reflection, starting from distinct positions. The four-robot case needed a separate geometric invariant [Bramas2018Four]. The point (gathering) and the regular polygon (uniform circle) are the only patterns formable from every initial configuration [Flocchini2017Uniform].

variants.title: ASYNC with common chirality
variants.summary: With common chirality, pattern formation and leader election are equivalent for $n \ge 4$.

results.note: Introductory and current best for the equivalence with chirality.

Patterns formable by oblivious ASYNC robots are exactly those formable by non-oblivious FSYNC robots, except a point of multiplicity 2. Its proof is reported as not correct by [Cicerone2019Asynchronous].

variants.notes: **Disputed:** the correctness of the proof of [Fujinaga2015Pattern] is questioned by [Cicerone2019Asynchronous]; it is shown as disputed and never as the current best.

variants.title: ASYNC with one common axis
variants.summary: With a common North and chirality, any odd number of robots forms any pattern; an even number cannot, in the worst case.

variants.title: ASYNC with a common compass
variants.summary: If robots agree on both axes, any number of robots forms any pattern.

variants.title: Randomized, ASYNC, no agreement
variants.summary: Randomness breaks symmetry: with one random bit per cycle, $n \ge 5$ robots form any pattern except gathering.

results.note: Patterns with multiplicity points are allowed, except gathering. Its proof is reported as not correct by [Cicerone2019Asynchronous].

variants.notes: Yamauchi and Yamashita gave a randomized algorithm with chirality (DISC 2014, not yet in the bibliography). **Disputed:** the proof of [Bramas2016Probabilistic] is questioned by [Cicerone2019Asynchronous]; no undisputed result is recorded for this setting.

variants.title: Opaque robots with lights, ASYNC, one axis, rigid
variants.summary: Opaque point robots with lights that agree on one axis form any pattern from the starts the paper characterises, with 6 colours.

results.note: Introductory and current best. Formation fails from starts symmetric about a robot-free line parallel to the agreed axis.

colours.note: No lower bound beyond trivial; the minimum is open.

open: The minimum number of colours, and formation with chirality only or with no agreement [Bose2021Opaque].

variants.title: Limited visibility
variants.summary: With limited visibility, oblivious robots form a pattern under the usual symmetry condition if they start within diameter 1; the general case is open.

assumes: initial diameter at most 1 (the visibility range)
results.note: Introductory and current best for oblivious robots.

open: Arbitrary pattern formation by oblivious robots with limited visibility from a general (connected) initial configuration [Hahn2024Large].

variants.title: Opaque robots with lights, ASYNC, compass, rigid
variants.summary: With a common compass, opaque robots with lights form any pattern with 3 colours.

variants.title: Opaque oblivious robots, ASYNC, compass
variants.summary: Without lights, opaque robots cannot form arbitrary patterns in ASYNC, even with a common compass.

preconditions: Theorem 1: oblivious opaque point robots, ASYNC
holds even with a common compass

variants.title: Opaque fat robots with lights, ASYNC, one axis
variants.summary: Opaque fat robots with lights that agree on one axis form any pattern from every start not symmetric about a robot-free line parallel to that axis, with 10 colours.

results.note: Introductory and current best. Theorem 1: solvable if and only if the start is not symmetric about a line parallel to the agreed axis through no robot centre. $\Theta(n)$ moves in total (Theorem 8), analysed under SSYNC with rigid moves.

variants.title: Fat robots with lights, FSYNC, randomized, no agreement
variants.summary: Randomized fat robots with lights and no common orientation form any pattern in FSYNC in $O(n)+O(\kappa\log n)$ rounds with probability at least $1-n^{-\kappa}$, with 7 colours.

assumes: the pattern is scaled by a constant (8 colours without scaling)
results.note: Introductory and current best (Theorems 11, 16, 20, 21); with probability at least $1-n^{-\kappa}$. Earlier versions used 10 and 11 colours.

variants.notes: With $O(1)$ words of $O(\log n)$ bits of persistent memory instead of lights, the same bound holds (Alsaedi, Gudmundsson and van Renssen, Computational Geometry 2025). Checked against the full text of [Alsaedi2025Pattern].

figure.caption: Pattern formation: $n$ oblivious robots at distinct points are given the same pattern $P$ in their local coordinate systems and must reach a configuration similar to $P$, up to translation, rotation and scaling [Suzuki1999Formation]. Shown, with chirality, the plan of [Dieudonne2010Leader] in SSYNC rounds: the smallest enclosing circle (dashed) gives the origin and unit, the ray to the leader $L$ (the robot nearest the centre) gives east; $P$ is placed accordingly (hollow points: the target points), and ringed (activated) robots walk to their target points one at a time without changing the circle or the leader; $L$ moves last.

frames.label: Start: SEC = unit circle; leader L fixes east
One robot at a time walks to its target point
Final: the robots form a copy of P
